entry.title: Big Rust Rewrites, 2025–2026
entry.content:
Big Rust Rewrites, 2025–2026¶

Published: Saturday, Nov 28, 2026 • 🏷️ rust

40 public Rust rewrites from Mar 2025 to Nov 2026, newest first. Eleven of the 24 from 2026 say AI agents wrote much of the code; in 2025 only Agoda (an AI-assisted prototype) and Microsoft’s research program mention AI at all.

Scope: rewrites or ports of an existing system, service or component, announced by the company or project itself. Most are big companies or major open-source toolchains; a few smaller projects (Ladybird, Mold, Prime Intellect, Momento, Goldsky, Radar, Spatie, LambdaWorks) are kept because they are widely cited.

Earlier posts on the topic: The State of “Let’s Rewrite It in Rust” (2025) and Microsoft Gets Rusty (2025).

Timeline¶

🤖 = AI-assisted, per the source. Names link to details. ⭐ in a Source line = detailed write-up worth reading in full.

Takeaways¶

Across the 40 rewrites, five patterns stand out.

  • Timing: agent-driven rewrites start in 2026 (11 of the 24 entries). The 2025 rewrites were done by hand, with AI at most for a prototype (Agoda) or as a research goal (Microsoft).
  • Verification: no team trusted the agents’ own tests. Each checked the new code against something independent:
    • Live traffic shadowed against the old system: Anthropic, Agoda.
    • Byte-identical output: Ladybird, Shopify (planned).
    • An existing test suite or behavioral harness the new code must pass: Bun (its TypeScript tests), Ladybird (test262), DataFusion Comet (Spark’s 24,000+ tests), tsrs (TypeScript conformance tests), React Compiler (1,725 fixtures), Spatie (parity-fix loop against Ray 3), LambdaWorks (compatibility contracts and versioned review workflows in Pogon).
    • Differential fuzzing against the old code: WhatsApp.
    • End-to-end tests added before porting started: GitHub.
  • Failures happen: Confluent restarted its agent-driven port after 3 months; Momento’s first Rust version did not cut latency by itself.
  • Why Rust: three main drivers show up repeatedly:
    • Memory and CPU cost (Anthropic, OpenAI, Grab, Agoda, AWS, Goldsky, LambdaWorks).
    • Memory safety on untrusted input in C/C++ parsers and system code (WhatsApp, Chrome fonts/PNG/XML, Pixel baseband DNS, Microsoft DirectWriteCore, Ubuntu sudo).
    • Replacing Node.js/JS developer tooling with native binaries (pnpm, Yarn 6, Vite 8 / Rolldown, Next.js Turbopack, React Compiler, tsrs, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot runtime) and Electron apps with GPUI (Discord, Spatie Ray 4).
  • Incremental vs. big-bang: most teams avoided a flag-day cutover and ran old and new side by side:
    • Component by component behind interop shims: GitHub Copilot runtime, LambdaWorks.
    • Opt-in first, default later: pnpm, Next.js Turbopack, Vite (Rolldown), Chrome PNG, Codex CLI.
    • Built in parallel, then swapped: WhatsApp, Agoda, Anthropic.
    • Big-bang ports were the exception, and only with a strong test suite as a safety net: Bun, Mold.

Rewrites¶

One snapshot per rewrite, in table order. Figures are as reported by each company.

Anthropic: Messages API¶

  • When: Nov 25, 2026
  • Status: Shipped, serving production traffic
  • What: The Claude Messages API service, rewritten from Python.
  • Why: Efficiency of the service that carries all Claude API traffic.
  • How: The existing Python service was the reference: production traffic was shadowed to the Rust version, and agent teams tracked down and fixed every difference.
  • Result: About 70% less CPU per request in one region, over 80% less memory per request, about 20% faster median time to first token.
  • By the numbers: First version in about 1 week; about 5 months of verification.
  • AI: Claude wrote the first version of the core path; agent teams handled the divergence fixes.
  • Source: Anthropic — ⭐ Must-read: content-blind shadow diffing grouped by fingerprint, replaying one model output to both stacks, why ~98% passing tests still meant ~25% production parity.

Confluent: Kafka client¶

  • When: Nov 24, 2026
  • Status: Released as Confluent’s Rust client (confluent-kafka crate)
  • What: A native Rust Kafka client translated from the Java client.
  • Why: Keep Confluent’s non-Java clients in step with the Java client.
  • How: A multi-agent translation workflow; engineers approve plans and make architecture calls, such as mapping Java threads to Tokio tasks.
  • Result: The first attempt was restarted; the goal is a continuous Java → Rust translation pipeline.
  • By the numbers: First attempt ran 3 months before the restart.
  • AI: Multi-agent workflow throughout.
  • Source: The New Stack and Confluent docs

Spatie: Ray 4¶

  • When: Nov 24, 2026
  • Status: Shipped
  • What: Ray, Spatie’s desktop debugging app, rewritten from Electron and React to Rust using Zed’s GPUI framework.
  • Why: Chromium’s baseline memory footprint limited how fast and light Ray could get, especially when receiving heavy log dumps.
  • How: Claude mapped all features from the Ray 3 codebase (manually validated by the team), built a GPUI component kit, and ran automated parity-fix loops against failing checks before 3 weeks of manual UI polish and code review.
  • Result: Ready to receive logs in 41 ms, ~194x faster handling 10,000 logs than Ray 3, ~4x less idle memory (~350 MB even after 10,000 logs), and a ~5x smaller download.
  • By the numbers: Five 7–8 hour agent loops in 1 week for the initial port; 4 weeks total vs an estimated 10 months by hand.
  • AI: Claude built the initial port and ran parity-fix loops, followed by manual polish and review agents.
  • Source: Spatie blog

Discord: desktop and mobile apps¶

  • When: Nov 4, 2026 (announced)
  • Status: In progress; user testing pending
  • What: Desktop leaves Electron; mobile drops React Native. Both share app code in Rust.
  • Why: Electron’s memory use, and one shared codebase for desktop and mobile. Discord has used Rust since 2018 in infrastructure, voice and parts of the client.
  • How: Desktop UI on GPUI, the GPU-accelerated framework from the makers of Zed (not Tauri); mobile keeps native UI on top of the shared Rust core.
  • Result: An early build used about 290 MB of RAM with two accounts signed in; today’s app often uses 1–4 GB.
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy’s post on X, reported by InfoQ

LambdaWorks: JVM microservices¶

  • When: Oct 29, 2026
  • Status: Shipped
  • What: Multiple separate JVM microservices consolidated into a single Rust modular monolith (one Rust package/process with shared PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, and HTTP mechanics).
  • Why: Higher throughput, leaner infrastructure, lower operating costs, fewer deployments, simpler CI, and easier maintenance.
  • How: Migrated service by service using Pogon, LambdaWorks’ internal AI software factory, with versioned migration skills, compatibility contracts, and automated review/check loops running between engineering sessions; engineers set scope and approved handoffs, updating the skills after each service.
  • Result: Server costs fell by about 70%; allocated production memory fell by 85.7%; fewer deployments and simpler CI.
  • AI: Coding agents orchestrated by Pogon handled implementation, automated checks, and review fixes within engineer-approved boundaries.
  • Source: LambdaWorks blog

Shopify: storefront renderer¶

  • When: Oct 2026 (announced)
  • Status: In progress
  • What: The storefront renderer, Ruby → Rust.
  • Why: Not stated.
  • How: The new renderer’s output is compared byte for byte with the Ruby one before switching over.
  • Result: None published yet.
  • AI: Implied: Lütke says Shopify engineers now work as “verification engineers”, building harnesses and acceptance tests.
  • Source: Vercel Ship 2026 recap. Tobi Lütke’s own words in the fireside “The Third Customer” (video published Oct 22, 2026); no Shopify blog post or GitHub repo found.

Cloudflare: tsrs TypeScript compiler¶

  • When: Oct 20, 2026
  • Status: Experimental release on npm (tsrs)
  • What: A Rust port of the TypeScript compiler, started by Max Schwenk at Owner.com and now developed by Cloudflare and VoidZero inside Oxc. Theo Browne’s tsc-rs port is being merged into it.
  • Why: Faster, lighter type checking, so AI agents and CI can check code cheaply; Rust also compiles to WebAssembly for browser and edge tools.
  • How: Agents ported the compiler; correctness is checked with TypeScript’s conformance tests, deliberately broken real projects, and Miri for memory bugs. Built in close collaboration with the TypeScript team, not as a fork.
  • Result: Up to 8x faster and 70% less memory than TypeScript 7.0, in Cloudflare’s benchmark.
  • AI: Written by agents with Claude Opus 5.5.
  • Source: Cloudflare blog and tsc-rs repo — ⭐ Must-read: read the tsc-rs repo: byte-for-byte conformance corpus, benchmark method, a documented known-differences list and a candid restart story.

Prime Intellect: Prime Agent¶

  • When: Oct 9, 2026
  • Status: Announced
  • What: The Prime Agent coding agent, rebuilt in Rust.
  • Why: Lower cold-start latency and memory use.
  • How: A large swarm of coding agents did the rebuild.
  • Result: Lower cold-start latency and memory use.
  • By the numbers: 2,000+ agents, 200B+ tokens, about 2 weeks.
  • AI: Agent swarm throughout.
  • Source: Prime Intellect blog — ⭐ Must-read: planner / implementer / adversarial reviewer / verifier pipeline, TUI frame diffing, a noise-checked performance hillclimb (vendor-run benchmarks).

Mold: linker¶

  • When: Oct 5, 2026 (v3.0.0)
  • Status: Shipped
  • What: The whole linker, C++ → Rust; 2.42.1 is the last C++ release.
  • Why: Rust had matured for systems software, and the project wants Linux distros to adopt mold as their default linker, including linker-script support.
  • How: A complete rewrite released as a drop-in replacement; Cargo replaces CMake and the oneTBB dependency is gone.
  • Result: Same options, targets and output apart from bug fixes; out-of-bounds reads now stop with a panic instead of corrupting memory.
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: mold 3.0.0 release notes

GitHub: Copilot runtime¶

  • When: Sep 16, 2026
  • Status: Shipped
  • What: The Copilot agent runtime behind the Copilot CLI, app and SDK, from TypeScript on Node.js to Rust with a C ABI.
  • Why: Every SDK consumer in every language had to ship Node.js or a bundled V8, on the order of 100 MB per client. Products needed in-process embedding, fast startup and low memory.
  • How: Incremental: components moved to Rust behind thin interop shims and shipped through 128 PRs to main, with no long-lived branch. Missing end-to-end tests were added before porting.
  • Result: The runtime now ships as a native binary; performance improved by orders of magnitude, per GitHub.
  • By the numbers: About 130K lines of TypeScript estimated at the start; 800K+ lines of Rust; about 14.5 weeks; mostly one developer; about $120K of tokens.
  • AI: Copilot agents wrote most of the code.
  • Source: GitHub blog — ⭐ Must-read: why in-place component-by-component on main beat big-bang and A/B, interop shim lifecycle, catalogue of real regressions.

OpenAI: Habitat storage¶

  • When: Sep 11, 2026
  • Status: Shipped; 95% of traffic on Rust
  • What: Habitat, the storage platform behind ChatGPT, from Python to Rust.
  • Why: Efficiency at ChatGPT scale.
  • How: A small team rebuilt the service with coding agents.
  • Result: 6x CPU and 15x memory efficiency.
  • By the numbers: 2 engineers, one quarter (Q2 2026).
  • AI: Codex with GPT-5.5.
  • Source: OpenAI

Google: Chrome XML parser¶

  • When: Sep 8, 2026 (Chrome 153)
  • Status: Shipped across Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS and Windows
  • What: Non-XSLT XML parsing in Chrome moved from libxml2 (C) to Rust.
  • Why: Eliminate memory corruption vulnerabilities in XML parsing while maintaining web-standards compatibility.
  • How: Replaced the C parser for non-XSLT paths (DOMParser, XMLHttpRequest.responseXML, and standalone/external SVG images) alongside Chrome’s XSLT deprecation.
  • Result: Removes memory corruption bug classes in standard XML and SVG parsing.
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: Chrome 153 release notes

pnpm: v12 package manager¶

  • When: Aug 26, 2026 (v12.0.0)
  • Status: Shipped
  • What: The pnpm package manager, rewritten from TypeScript on Node.js to Rust (codenamed pacquet).
  • Why: Eliminate Node.js runtime startup overhead and speed up filesystem-heavy installs and dependency resolution.
  • How: Developed as pacquet, merged into the main pnpm monorepo in May 2026, and rolled out incrementally as an opt-in backend across v11.2–v11.10 before becoming stable in v12.0.0.
  • Result: Ships as native per-platform binaries with deterministic lockfiles; large workspaces with cyclic dependencies resolve peers 2–3x faster with about 25% less memory.
  • AI: Not stated in the release post.
  • Source: pnpm 12.0 release blog

DataFusion Comet: Spark execution¶

  • When: Aug 7, 2026 (v1.0.0)
  • Status: Shipped (1.2.0 by Nov 2026)
  • What: A Spark plugin that moves query execution from the JVM to Rust (Apache DataFusion); Spark stays the coordinator. Started at Apple, donated to Apache in March 2024.
  • Why: JVM limits in Spark: garbage-collection overhead and row-by-row execution.
  • How: Translates Spark physical plans into DataFusion plans with no code changes, and falls back to Spark for anything not supported. Runs Spark’s own test suite in CI.
  • Result: 2x speedup on 1 TB TPC-DS, about 50% lower infrastructure cost (Google Cloud community benchmark). Apple runs it on its petabyte-scale Iceberg lakehouse.
  • By the numbers: 1.0 had 244 commits from 23 contributors; 24,000+ Spark unit tests in CI.
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: Apache DataFusion blog

Bun: runtime¶

  • When: Jul 8, 2026 (merged May 14, shipped in v1.4.0)
  • Status: Shipped
  • What: The whole runtime, Zig → Rust. Bun is owned by Anthropic and runs Claude Code.
  • Why: Most of Bun’s crash bugs were use-after-free, double-free and missed frees; in safe Rust these are compile errors, and Drop handles cleanup.
  • How: A mechanical port with as few behavior changes as possible, driven by a PORTING.md rulebook. Bun’s test suite is written in TypeScript, so it served as an independent conformance check.
  • Result: 128 long-standing bugs fixed; live in Claude Code since v2.1.181, with 10% faster startup on Linux.
  • By the numbers: About 535K lines of Zig; 11 days; up to 64 agent instances in parallel.
  • AI: An agent harness with a pre-release Claude model.
  • Source: Bun blog — ⭐ Must-read: the case for an all-at-once mechanical port, adversarial diff-only review, agents clobbering each other’s git state.

Meta: React Compiler¶

  • When: Jul 2026
  • Status: Experimental, merged into the React repo
  • What: React Compiler, TypeScript → Rust.
  • Why: Faster builds and direct use inside Rust-based JavaScript tools such as Turbopack, Oxc and SWC, without a Babel step.
  • How: A port that keeps a Babel-like public API, so upgrading needs no config changes.
  • Result: About 3x faster as a Babel plugin, up to 10x for the transform; all 1,725 test fixtures pass.
  • AI: “Majority coded by AI”, architecture set by humans.
  • Source: React pull request #36173 — ⭐ Must-read: porting a compiler pass by pass, with intermediate state compared after every pass; arenas and indices for the borrow checker.

Goldsky: streaming pipelines¶

  • When: Jun 2026
  • Status: Shipped and open-sourced (Streamling)
  • What: Streaming pipelines moved from Apache Flink to Streamling, Goldsky’s own Rust runtime.
  • Why: Flink was hard for anyone outside the streaming core team to extend, and the AWS bill was high.
  • How: A new runtime built on Rust, Apache Arrow and DataFusion.
  • Result: Average CPU from 10+ cores to 0.3 in a Kafka-to-ClickHouse workload.
  • By the numbers: Over $1M a year saved.
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: Goldsky blog

Google: Pixel baseband DNS parser¶

  • When: Apr 10, 2026
  • Status: Shipped in Pixel 10 modem firmware
  • What: The DNS packet parser inside Google Pixel’s cellular baseband firmware, C → Rust (hickory-proto).
  • Why: Cellular modems run tens of megabytes of predominantly memory-unsafe firmware on untrusted network packets, making C DNS parsers a high-value remote attack surface.
  • How: Adopted the open-source hickory-proto crate and contributed upstream no_std support across hickory-dns, rust-url and ipnet so it could run in a bare-metal firmware environment behind a thin Rust shim.
  • Result: Eliminates memory-safety vulnerability classes in cellular DNS parsing; adds 371 KB total code size (4 KB shim, 17 KB core/alloc/builtins, 350 KB library).
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: Google Security Blog — ⭐ Must-read: Rust in bare-metal firmware: rlibs wrapped in one staticlib, a compiler_builtins memcpy regression, allocator and panic glue.

Vite: Vite 8 / Rolldown¶

  • When: Mar 12, 2026 (v8.0)
  • Status: Shipped
  • What: Vite replaced its dual-bundler core—esbuild (Go) for dev and Rollup (JS) for production—with Rolldown, a single Rust bundler built on Oxc.
  • Why: Maintaining two separate transformation pipelines and plugin systems created glue code and edge-case drift, while Rollup’s JavaScript performance bottlenecked large builds.
  • How: Built Rolldown with Rollup/Vite plugin API compatibility and an automatic config compatibility layer, previewed as rolldown-vite on Vite 7 before becoming the default in Vite 8.
  • Result: 10–30x faster than Rollup in benchmarks (matching esbuild’s speed); adds ~15 MB to install size (~10 MB from lightningcss, ~5 MB from Rolldown).
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: Vite 8.0 announcement

Ladybird: LibJS frontend¶

  • When: Feb 23, 2026
  • Status: Shipped in Ladybird
  • What: The JavaScript engine’s lexer, parser and bytecode generator, C++ → Rust.
  • Why: Ladybird adopted Rust for memory safety in new and ported code.
  • How: A human-directed port with coding agents; the new code had to produce identical output to the C++ version.
  • Result: Zero regressions on 52,898 test262 tests and 12,461 of Ladybird’s own.
  • By the numbers: About 25K lines in about 2 weeks.
  • AI: Claude Code and Codex.
  • Source: Ladybird blog

Meta: messaging library¶

  • When: Feb 10, 2026
  • Status: Not stated
  • What: A core cross-platform messaging library, C → Rust.
  • Why: Not stated in writing; discussed on the podcast.
  • How: Not stated in writing.
  • Result: No figures published.
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: Meta Tech Podcast

Yarn: Yarn 6¶

  • When: Jan 28, 2026 (preview; 6.0.0-rc.23 by Oct 2026)
  • Status: Release candidate (yarnpkg/zpm)
  • What: The Yarn package manager, rewritten from TypeScript on Node.js to Rust.
  • Why: Higher responsiveness, lower memory use, and standalone binary distribution (Yarn Switch) without Node.js startup overhead.
  • How: Rewritten over more than a year in the yarnpkg/zpm repository, with Yarn 5.x serving as the JavaScript transition bridge and long-term maintenance line.
  • Result: Warm-cache Next.js install dropped from 577 ms (legacy Yarn) to 184 ms in Yarn’s preview benchmark.
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: Yarn 6 Preview blog and Maël Nison’s announcement

WhatsApp: media library¶

  • When: Jan 27, 2026
  • Status: Shipped on Android, iOS, web, wearables and more
  • What: wamedia, the library that checks shared media files, C++ → Rust.
  • Why: Media checks run automatically on untrusted input. The 2015 Stagefright bug in Android’s media libraries showed how dangerous that is.
  • How: Not an incremental rewrite: the Rust version was built in parallel with the C++ one and checked against it with differential fuzzing plus integration and unit tests.
  • Result: 160K lines of C++ became 90K lines of Rust.
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: Engineering at Meta

X: For You algorithm¶

  • When: Jan 20, 2026
  • Status: In production for the For You feed; migration partial
  • What: The “For You” feed algorithm, rebuilt in Rust and Python to replace the 2023 Scala version.
  • Why: Not stated.
  • How: A ground-up rebuild around a Grok-based ranking model, published as open source.
  • Result: The open-source repo was still about 24% Scala in Aug 2026.
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: xai-org/x-algorithm on GitHub

Microsoft: research program¶

  • When: Dec 2025
  • Status: Goal / research
  • What: A research program to move Microsoft’s C and C++ code to Rust by 2030.
  • Why: Remove the memory-safety bugs that C and C++ allow.
  • How: AI agents guided by algorithms, aiming at “1 engineer, 1 month, 1 million lines” (Galen Hunt).
  • Result: None yet; Microsoft says Windows is not being rewritten.
  • AI: Planned as the core of the approach.
  • Source: The Register, reporting Hunt’s LinkedIn post

Vercel: Next.js 16 / Turbopack¶

  • When: Oct 21, 2025 (Next.js 16)
  • Status: Shipped as default bundler
  • What: Turbopack, Vercel’s Rust-based incremental bundler, became the default bundler for Next.js, replacing Webpack (JavaScript).
  • Why: Faster development refresh and production builds on large React applications through fine-grained incremental computation.
  • How: Rolled out opt-in across Next.js 15 (reaching >50% of dev sessions and 20% of production builds on 15.3+) before becoming default in Next.js 16, with --webpack kept as an escape hatch.
  • Result: 2–5x faster production builds and up to 10x faster Fast Refresh.
  • AI: No.
  • Source: Next.js 16 blog and Next.js 15.5 blog

Canonical: Ubuntu sudo and coreutils¶

  • When: Oct 2025 (Ubuntu 25.10)
  • Status: Shipped
  • What: sudo and coreutils replaced by Rust versions.
  • Why: Memory safety in core system tools.
  • How: Adopted existing Rust projects, sudo-rs and uutils coreutils, rather than writing new ones.
  • Result: First major distro to make sudo-rs the default.
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: Ubuntu Discourse

Agoda: Feature Store¶

  • When: Oct 8, 2025
  • Status: Shipped
  • What: Feature Store serving, Scala → Rust.
  • Why: Latency problems and scaling bottlenecks on the JVM.
  • How: A 1-week proof of concept first; shadow testing against the Scala service before production.
  • Result: 84% lower cost while handling 5x more traffic.
  • By the numbers: CPU at 40% and memory at 15% of Scala levels.
  • AI: The proof of concept was built with AI tools by a team with no Rust experience.
  • Source: Agoda Engineering

Cloudflare: FL2 proxy¶

  • When: Sep 26, 2025
  • Status: Shipped
  • What: FL, the core proxy layer, from NGINX and LuaJIT to Rust (FL2).
  • Why: Speed and security of the layer every request passes through.
  • How: A new proxy, FL2, replaced the NGINX/LuaJIT-based FL.
  • Result: 10 ms faster at the median; 25% performance boost.
  • AI: No.
  • Source: Cloudflare blog — ⭐ Must-read: Rust modules inside the old NGINX first, the Flamingo FL1-vs-FL2 test system, raw-byte fallback to the old proxy.

Microsoft: DirectWriteCore¶

  • When: Sep 2025 (reported at RustConf 2025)
  • Status: Shipped in Windows
  • What: DirectWriteCore, Windows’ text-rendering and font-shaping subsystem, C++ → Rust.
  • Why: Memory safety in font parsing and rendering.
  • How: Targeted subsystem rewrite inside Windows rather than a full OS rewrite.
  • Result: 5–15% faster font shaping.
  • By the numbers: 154,000 lines of Rust; 2 engineers; 6 months.
  • AI: No.
  • Source: Mark Russinovich’s RustConf 2025 keynote

Proton: Mail mobile apps¶

  • When: Sep 2025 (launch; write-up in 2026)
  • Status: Shipped
  • What: A complete rewrite of the Proton Mail iOS and Android apps; business logic moved from Kotlin and Swift into one Rust core.
  • Why: Duplicated work and feature gaps between the iOS and Android teams. React Native, Flutter and Kotlin Multiplatform were tested first and rejected.
  • How: Native UI on each platform (Jetpack Compose, SwiftUI) on top of a shared Rust core that holds all business logic, down to navigation.
  • Result: Almost 80% of code shared across platforms; 12 feature releases in the 2 months after launch.
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: Proton blog

Momento: data plane¶

  • When: 2025 (conference talks)
  • Status: Shipped; all services moved from Kotlin to Rust
  • What: The serverless cache’s data plane, Kotlin → Rust.
  • Why: Unpredictable tail latencies on the JVM.
  • How: Storage layer first, then the routing layer, then remaining services, ending with a complex workflow server.
  • Result: The first Rust version did not cut latency by itself; the team later reported Rust did not slow them down as they had feared.
  • By the numbers: About 3 years from first to last service.
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: Talk by Momento’s Ramya Krishnamoorthy on InfoQ and follow-up talk by Ruth Linehan — ⭐ Must-read: the first talk: p999 benchmark method, debugging an h2 mutex bottleneck from 32K to 75K TPS, a minor tonic upgrade that took prod down.

Google: Chrome PNG decoder¶

  • When: Aug 2025 (Chrome 139; legacy flag removed in M142, Oct 2025)
  • Status: Shipped
  • What: Chrome’s Blink and Skia PNG decoding moved from libpng (C) to the Rust png crate (SkPngRustDecoder).
  • Why: Eliminate memory-safety vulnerabilities when decoding untrusted PNG images from the web.
  • How: Shipped behind chrome://flags/#rusty-png while closing edge-case parity bugs, then made default in M139 and followed by systematically removing libpng dependencies from Blink and Skia.
  • Result: Memory-safe PNG decoding in production across Chromium; libpng references stripped from Blink and Skia.
  • AI: No.
  • Source: Chromium issue #443128323 and Chromium Security Quarterly Updates

Radar: geocoding¶

  • When: Aug 7, 2025
  • Status: Shipped
  • What: Geocoding moved off Elasticsearch, MongoDB and several microservices onto HorizonDB, one Rust service.
  • Why: Scaling Elasticsearch meant hard JVM tuning; the team wanted linear scaling on commodity hardware and easy local development.
  • How: Built on RocksDB, S2, Tantivy and FSTs; data preprocessed in Spark and stored as versioned assets in S3.
  • Result: A single multi-threaded process with predictable latency.
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: Radar blog

OpenAI: Codex CLI¶

  • When: Jun 2025
  • Status: Shipped; Rust is the default and only maintained version
  • What: Codex CLI, TypeScript on Node.js → Rust.
  • Why: Zero-dependency install (Node v22+ was required), native security bindings for sandboxing, and an extensible protocol.
  • How: The Rust version shipped side by side as a separate npm tag until it matched the TypeScript one, then became the default.
  • Result: No Node.js install needed; native OS sandboxing.
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: Codex GitHub discussion #1174

Microsoft: SymCrypt¶

  • When: Jun 2025
  • Status: In progress (research)
  • What: SymCrypt, Microsoft’s cryptographic library, being rewritten in Rust.
  • Why: Modernize a core crypto library with memory safety.
  • How: Not stated here.
  • Result: No figures published.
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: Microsoft Research blog

Grab: Counter Service¶

  • When: 2025
  • Status: Shipped
  • What: Counter Service, Go → Rust.
  • Why: Infrastructure cost.
  • How: A rewrite of one high-traffic Go service.
  • Result: Similar performance at much lower cost.
  • By the numbers: 20 cores down to 4.5; 70% infrastructure savings.
  • AI: No.
  • Source: Grab Engineering — ⭐ Must-read: black-box rewrite against the gRPC contract (no line-by-line, no C2Rust), library choices, a sync Redis call inside async code.

Meta: Pyrefly¶

  • When: May 15, 2025 (alpha open-sourced)
  • Status: Shipped (open-source, MIT license)
  • What: A Python type checker and IDE extension written in Rust to succeed Meta’s OCaml-based Pyre.
  • Why: High-speed incremental checking across large monorepos and a unified cross-platform developer experience.
  • How: Built from the ground up in Rust with incremental updates and open-sourced under the MIT license.
  • Result: Checks up to 1.8 million lines of code per second on large codebases.
  • AI: Not stated.
  • Source: Engineering at Meta

AWS: Aurora DSQL¶

  • When: May 2025
  • Status: Shipped
  • What: The Aurora DSQL database, Kotlin → Rust.
  • Why: The tuned Kotlin version hit JVM warm-up and garbage-collection limits.
  • How: A rewrite of the data plane after the Kotlin version was tuned as far as it would go.
  • Result: 30,000 TPS vs 2,000–3,000 for tuned Kotlin; Rust later became AWS’s default for data plane projects.
  • By the numbers: About 10x throughput.
  • AI: No.
  • Source: All Things Distributed — ⭐ Must-read: what was rewritten first and why, reversing the Kotlin control-plane decision, Rust types encoding Postgres C invariants.

Google: Chrome fonts¶

  • When: Mar 19, 2025
  • Status: Shipped
  • What: Chrome’s font processing moved from FreeType (C) to Skrifa (Rust).
  • Why: Font-parsing security bugs had repeatedly reached users.
  • How: Replaced FreeType with Skrifa, a Rust library, inside Chrome.
  • Result: Removes whole classes of font vulnerabilities.
  • AI: No.
  • Source: Chrome for Developers blog — ⭐ Must-read: staged FreeType → Skrifa rollout, keeping unsafe to bytemuck, differential outline and pixel testing plus fuzzing.

entry.title: Go Parallel Builds: 14 Binaries, One go build
entry.content:
Go Parallel Builds: 14 Binaries, One go build¶

Published: Friday, Nov 27, 2026 • 🏷️ golang • ci • make

TL;DR¶

  • One go build instead of 14: the build step in our CI went from 78s to 17s (median of 5 runs each).
  • Whole CI job: 152s → 76–97s (one run before the change, 3 runs after).
  • No tuning needed: the default -p was as fast as anything I set by hand.
  • Same lesson in tests: our go test run is build-bound. 39s of a 49s warm run is compile and link, and only ~15s is test execution.

The Problem¶

Our Go monorepo ships 14 binaries: three web portals, a handful of queue workers, a CLI and some e2e helpers. The build-apps CI job built them in a loop, one go build per binary, then ran --help on each one as a smoke test.

# before (simplified)
build-apps:
    for app in $(APPS); do \
        go build -ldflags="$(LDFLAGS)" -o build/$$app ./apps/$$app || exit 1; \
    done

The build cache was warm, so the shared packages weren’t recompiled. The job still took 152s, and the build steps alone took 81s. Every iteration loads the package graph again, checks the cache again, and links one big static binary, while the rest of the 8-CPU CircleCI large executor sits idle.

The Fix¶

go build accepts many main packages at once. With -o pointing at a directory (trailing slash), it writes one binary per package, named after the last element of its import path.

# No -p: defaults to GOMAXPROCS.
build-binaries:
    env CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 \
        go build -ldflags="$(LDFLAGS)" -o build/ \
        $(foreach a,$(BUILT_APPS),./apps/$(a)) $(E2E_TOOL_PKGS)

Why not just go build -o build/ ./apps/...? It builds the same 11 apps, but the e2e tools live outside apps/ (./testing/e2e/report, gotest.tools/gotestsum), and a release builds just the one app it deploys. An explicit list covers both.

In CircleCI, 11 build steps, 10 verify steps and a “Build e2e tools” step (3 more binaries) became one make build-binaries verify-binaries step. A separate verify-binaries target still runs --help on each app. Output paths and ldflags stayed the same, so the Dockerfiles didn’t change.

I measured it on the same commit and cache, with 5 CI runs per variant:

Variant Median Range
Serial loop (before) 78s 71–98s
-p 2 39s 34–42s
-p 4 21s 20–28s
-p 6 17s 13–22s
Default (-p = GOMAXPROCS = 8) 17s 16–20s

Why It Works¶

  • One package graph. A single invocation loads and resolves the module graph once. Shared packages are compiled (or fetched from the cache) once and reused by every binary.
  • Parallel actions. go build schedules compile and link actions on a worker pool of size -p. In the loop, every link waited for the previous binary. Now up to 8 links run at the same time.
  • Default -p is right. -p defaults to GOMAXPROCS, and since Go 1.25 GOMAXPROCS follows the container’s CPU quota. On CircleCI large that’s 8. My runs showed -p 4 slower and -p 6 no faster than the default, so the Makefile sets nothing.
  • Linking dominates a warm build. With a warm cache there is little left to compile, and linking 14 static binaries is the real work. It parallelizes well: -p 2 halves the time and -p 4 nearly quarters it.

To see where the time goes, go build -debug-actiongraph=out.json (an undocumented debug flag) dumps every action with its start and end time. Here are the same 14 binaries, built both ways on my laptop:

Wall clock (laptop) Before (14 builds) After (1 build)
Load packages 7s 0.7s
Cache checks 10s (22,119 checks) 1s (2,108 checks)
Link 30s, one at a time 10s, side by side
Total 47s 11s

Loading and checking the packages once saves about 15s. Running the links side by side saves about 20s. In the chart, the ops-cli tail is waiting for a free worker. (The binary names are anonymized.)

The Appendix shows how to record and read these action graphs for your own repo.

The Same Lesson in Tests¶

After the build fix I looked at go test with the same eyes. Our unit test run is mostly a build, too:

Run Time
Warm run, default flags (-p 8) 49s (39s build and link, ~15s summed test time)
-p 2 77s
-p 1 144s
-parallel 1 (no t.Parallel inside a package) 49s
Cold build and test 5m04s
make test-be repeated (test cache) 9s

The build and test times overlap (packages start testing while others still build), so 39s + 15s adds up to more than 49s.

-p controls how many packages are built and tested at once, and it moves the needle a lot. -parallel controls how many t.Parallel() tests run at once inside one package, and it changed nothing. We have 2,130 t.Parallel() calls, and they don’t buy speed here. What they buy is race coverage: with -race, they catch races on state shared between tests.

So the fix for slow tests is the same as for slow builds: keep the build cache warm and let go use all the CPUs. Splitting tests across more jobs would mostly rebuild the same packages several times. I’ll cover keeping the cache warm in the next post.

When NOT to Use It¶

Situation Use one go build?
Many binaries sharing packages, same GOOS/GOARCH and ldflags ✅
Binaries need different build tags or CGO_ENABLED ❌ Group them by flags, one invocation per group
Cross-compiling for several platforms ❌ One invocation per GOOS/GOARCH (they can still run in parallel)
You need to know which binary failed to compile ✅ The error still names the failing package
1–2 CPU runner ⚠️ It still helps, but expect 2×, not 4×
Runner with little memory per CPU ⚠️ Parallel links add up in RAM; cap -p if the job gets OOM-killed
Binaries from different modules (nested go.mod) ❌ go build works per module

Parallel links cost memory: each one loads the whole program. On my 16 GB laptop, 10 concurrent links peaked at about 12 GB RSS, against 2.4 GB for the serial loop, and each link slowed from ~3s to ~7s (~16s once the laptop was swapping). Check the executor’s RAM before you rely on the default -p.

Key Takeaways¶

  • Pass all main packages to one go build -o dir/. The build step went from 78s to 17s.
  • Don’t hand-tune -p. GOMAXPROCS already follows the container quota.
  • Measure before you parallelize tests. Ours were build-bound, and t.Parallel() gave race coverage, not speed.
  • Keep a cheap smoke test (--help) right after the build so a broken binary fails fast.

References¶

  • go help build: the -o directory and -p flags
  • Go 1.25 release notes: container-aware GOMAXPROCS
  • go help testflag: -parallel vs -p
  • Standardizing Go Build Systems Across 15 Microservices with Claude Code
  • common-make: Zero-Setup Build Automation for Go Services

Appendix: Check Your Own Repo¶

Build once to warm the cache. Then record one action graph per go build in the loop, and one for the single build:

mkdir -p ag/before
# before: one go build per main package
for app in $(go list -f '{{if eq .Name "main"}}{{.Dir}}{{end}}' ./apps/...); do
  go build -debug-actiongraph=ag/before/$(basename $app).json -o build/ $app
done
# after: one go build for all of them
go build -debug-actiongraph=ag/after.json -o build/ ./apps/...

actiongraph reads these files. types sums the time per action type. Merge the “before” files with jq first:

go install github.com/icio/actiongraph@latest
jq -s add ag/before/*.json | actiongraph types
actiongraph types -f ag/after.json

# our numbers, before: 14 go builds
 76.166s  63.22%  build check cache
 29.788s  24.73%  link
 14.513s  12.05%  build

# our numbers, after: 1 go build
 74.782s  89.45%  link
  7.243s   8.66%  build check cache
  1.563s   1.87%  build

types adds up the duration of every action, so actions that overlap are counted more than once. Read these numbers as worker time, not wall-clock time. The table in Why It Works is wall-clock time from the same files.

To get a timeline like the chart in Why It Works, record with -debug-trace=trace.json as well and open the file in Perfetto. It shows one lane per worker, so you can see the links running side by side.

entry.title: devbox: Personal Makefile Extensions Without Team Conflicts
entry.content:
devbox: Personal Makefile Extensions Without Team Conflicts¶

Published: Monday, Jun 29, 2026 • 🏷️ make • devex

TL;DR¶

devbox is a pattern for extending project Makefiles with personal development workflows without polluting team repositories.

Key benefits:

  • Personal targets (e.g., rbk build-proc, rbk run-main, rbk run-worker - define any targets you need) coexist with team targets (make test, make build)
  • No git history pollution - extensions live in separate repo, symlinked to projects
  • Shared utilities (credentials, env files, scripts) across multiple services
  • Zero impact on team workflow

Standardizing Makefiles across teams is good (common-make), but some requirements are too specific to personal dev flow. devbox lets you extend, not replace.

Each service gets its own devbox Makefile that you can freely customize with targets specific to that service’s architecture (event processors, workers, multiple apps, etc.).

The Problem: When Personal Needs Diverge¶

After standardizing build systems with common-make, I needed:

  • Multiple env configs per service (.env.test, .env.local, .env.proc)
  • Quick rebuilds without full test suite (build-main, build-proc)
  • Shared credentials and helper scripts across 10+ microservices
  • Custom environment variable loading

These are valuable for personal productivity but don’t belong in the team’s Makefile.

The Solution: devbox Pattern¶

devbox is a separate git repository that extends project Makefiles via symlinks:

~/Projects/company/
├── devbox/                    # Personal tooling repo
│   ├── Makefile_devbox        # Common devbox targets
│   ├── _scripts/              # Shared utilities
│   │   ├── env-args.sh        # Load env files (key utility!)
│   │   ├── db-tunnel.sh       # SSH tunnel to remote DB
│   │   ├── get-credentials.sh # Fetch from secret store
│   │   └── jwt-decode.sh      # Debug auth tokens
│   ├── service-a/             # Per-service customization
│   │   ├── Makefile           # Service-specific devbox targets
│   │   ├── .env               # Local environment config
│   │   └── .env.proc          # Event processor config
│   └── service-b/
│       ├── Makefile
│       └── .env
│
├── service-a/
│   ├── Makefile               # Team's standard Makefile
│   └── .devbox -> ../devbox   # Symlink (gitignored)
│
└── service-b/
    ├── Makefile
    └── .devbox -> ../devbox

How It Works¶

1. The rbk Alias¶

Add to your shell profile (~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc):

alias rbk='f(){ (cd . && make -f .devbox/$(pwd | xargs basename)/Makefile "$@");  unset -f f; }; f'

2. Three-Layer Makefile Architecture¶

Example:

# In devbox/service-a/Makefile

include .devbox/Makefile_devbox        # Layer 1: Common devbox targets
include $(CURR_DIR)/Makefile           # Layer 2: Team's standard Makefile

## Layer 3: Service-specific devbox targets

EVENT_PROCESSOR_NAME := event-processor
EVENT_PROCESSOR_DIR := ./cmd/$(EVENT_PROCESSOR_NAME)

.PHONY: build-proc
build-proc: ## Build event-processor (no tests)
    CGO_ENABLED=0 go build $(BUILD_FLAGS) -ldflags="$(LINK_FLAGS)" \
        -o build/$(EVENT_PROCESSOR_NAME) $(EVENT_PROCESSOR_DIR)

.PHONY: run-proc
run-proc: build-proc  ## Run event-processor with .env.proc
    $(shell $(DBOX_DIR_NAME)/_scripts/env-args.sh \
        $(DBOX_DIR_NAME)/$(SUB_DUR)/.env.proc) \
        build/$(EVENT_PROCESSOR_NAME) consume --adapter nakadi

Result: You get both team targets (make test) and personal targets (rbk run-proc).

Each service can have completely different devbox targets based on its architecture. One service might have build-proc and run-proc for event processing, another might have build-worker for background jobs, or build-cli for command-line tools. You define whatever makes sense for each service.

3. Environment File Loading: env-args.sh¶

The key utility - dead simple env file loader without overengineering:

#!/bin/bash
# devbox/_scripts/env-args.sh

ENV_FILE_PATH=$1
env cat $ENV_FILE_PATH | egrep -v "(^#.*|^$)" | xargs -0 | tr '\n' ' '

Usage in Makefile:

run-proc: build-proc
    $(shell .devbox/_scripts/env-args.sh .devbox/service-a/.env.proc) \
        build/event-processor consume

Setup Instructions¶

Initial Setup¶

  1. Create devbox repository:

    cd ~/Projects/company
mkdir devbox && cd devbox
git init

  2. Create base structure:

    Create Makefile_devbox:

    .DEFAULT_GOAL := help
CURR_DIR := $(shell pwd)
DBOX_DIR_NAME := .devbox
SUB_DUR := $(shell pwd | xargs basename)

.PHONY: env
env: ## Show environment info
    @echo CURR_DIR=$(CURR_DIR)
    @echo DBOX_DIR_NAME=$(DBOX_DIR_NAME)
    $(shell env cat $(DBOX_DIR_NAME)/$(SUB_DUR)/.env | xargs -0)

    Create _scripts/env-args.sh:

    #!/bin/bash
ENV_FILE_PATH=$1
env cat $ENV_FILE_PATH | egrep -v "(^#.*|^$)" | xargs -0 | tr '\n' ' '

    chmod +x _scripts/env-args.sh

  3. Add rbk alias:

    echo "alias rbk='f(){ (cd . && make -f .devbox/\$(pwd | xargs basename)/Makefile \"\$@\");  unset -f f; }; f'" >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc

Add Service to devbox¶

For each service you want to extend:

cd ~/Projects/company/devbox
mkdir service-a

Create service-a/Makefile:

include .devbox/Makefile_devbox
include $(CURR_DIR)/Makefile

APP_NAME := app
APP_DIR := ./cmd/$(APP_NAME)

.PHONY: build-main
build-main: ## Build main app (no tests)
    CGO_ENABLED=0 go build $(BUILD_FLAGS) -ldflags="$(LINK_FLAGS)" \
        -o build/$(APP_NAME) $(APP_DIR)

.PHONY: run-main
run-main: build-main  ## Run with .env
    $(shell $(DBOX_DIR_NAME)/_scripts/env-args.sh \
        $(DBOX_DIR_NAME)/$(SUB_DUR)/.env) build/$(APP_NAME)

Create service-a/.env:

# Local development environment
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_USER=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=postgres
DB_NAME=service_a_test
ADDRESS=localhost:8080
ENABLE_TRACING=true

Link from service to devbox:

cd ~/Projects/company/devbox
ln -s $(pwd) ~/Projects/company/service-a/.devbox

Verify Setup¶

cd ~/Projects/company/service-a

# Test team's standard targets (still work!)
make test
make build

# Test devbox targets
rbk help        # Shows both team and devbox targets
rbk env         # Shows your custom environment
rbk build-main  # Quick build without tests
rbk run-main    # Run with your .env

When NOT to Use devbox¶

Don’t use devbox for:

  • Targets that everyone on team needs (add to team Makefile)
  • Production deployment logic (belongs in team’s CI/CD)
  • Anything that should be standardized across team

DO use devbox for:

  • Personal iteration shortcuts
  • Local-only configurations
  • Development convenience targets
  • Cross-service helper scripts

Conclusion¶

devbox lets you extend standardized Makefiles without forcing personal preferences on the team. Standardize the foundation, extend where workflows diverge.

References¶

Related Blog Posts¶

  • common-make: Zero-Setup Build Automation for Go Services
  • Standardizing Go Build Systems Across 15 Microservices with Claude Code

Key Files¶

  • devbox/Makefile_devbox - Common devbox targets
  • devbox/_scripts/env-args.sh - Simple env file loader
  • devbox/<service>/Makefile - Per-service extensions

entry.title: Go Vanity Import Paths
entry.content:
Go Vanity Import Paths¶

Published: Thursday, Jun 04, 2026 • 🏷️ golang

I’ve been seeing these import paths in Go projects:

  • go.uber.org/zap
  • k8s.io/client-go
  • go.opentelemetry.io/otel
  • google.golang.org/grpc

These aren’t GitHub URLs. How does Go resolve them? I decided to investigate.

The Investigation¶

First, I checked what these domains actually return:

$ curl go.uber.org/zap
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
    <head>
        <meta name="go-import" content="go.uber.org/zap git https://github.com/uber-go/zap">
        <meta name="go-source" content="go.uber.org/zap https://github.com/uber-go/zap https://github.com/uber-go/zap/tree/master{/dir} https://github.com/uber-go/zap/tree/master{/dir}/{file}#L{line}">
        <meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0; url=https://pkg.go.dev/go.uber.org/zap">
    </head>
    <body>
        Nothing to see here. Please <a href="https://pkg.go.dev/go.uber.org/zap">move along</a>.
    </body>
</html>

Interesting. Just HTML with meta tags pointing to GitHub. Same pattern everywhere.

The Official Docs¶

Found the explanation in Remote import paths:

If the import path is not a known code hosting site and also lacks a version control qualifier, the go tool attempts to fetch the import over https/http and looks for a <meta> tag in the document’s HTML <head>.

The meta tag has the form:

<meta name="go-import" content="import-prefix vcs repo-root">

Note: Go adds ?go-get=1 to the request so servers can distinguish between Go tooling and regular browsers.

So the flow is:

  1. Go requests https://go.uber.org/zap?go-get=1
  2. Parses go-import meta tag from HTML <head>
  3. Clones from actual repository: https://github.com/uber-go/zap

Simple HTTP + HTML meta tags. No magic.

Who Uses This¶

I checked several major Go projects:

  • Kubernetes - k8s.io/* → github.com/kubernetes/*
  • gRPC - google.golang.org/grpc → github.com/grpc/grpc-go
  • Uber - go.uber.org/* → github.com/uber-go/*
  • OpenTelemetry - go.opentelemetry.io/* → github.com/open-telemetry/*
  • etcd - go.etcd.io/* → github.com/etcd-io/etcd
  • Knative - knative.dev/* → github.com/knative/*

All large organizations with many packages. Makes sense - if you’re managing 20+ Go repos, a custom domain gives you VCS flexibility.

The Go Implementation¶

I wanted to see how Go actually implements this. Found it in the Go source at src/cmd/go/internal/vcs/:

Building the URL (vcs.go):

func urlForImportPath(importPath string) (*url.URL, error) {
    host, path := splitPath(importPath)
    return &url.URL{Host: host, Path: path, RawQuery: "go-get=1"}, nil
}

Turns go.uber.org/zap → https://go.uber.org/zap?go-get=1.

Parsing HTML (discovery.go):

func parseMetaGoImports(r io.Reader) ([]metaImport, error) {
    decoder := xml.NewDecoder(r)
    decoder.Strict = false // Lenient parsing

    // Scan for <meta name="go-import" content="...">
    // Stop at </head> or <body>
}

Key details: case-insensitive HTML parsing, only scans <head> section, caches results, and has built-in patterns for GitHub/Bitbucket.

How to Implement It¶

Option 1: Static HTML (what most orgs use)

Host a simple HTML file on your custom domain:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <meta name="go-import" content="example.com/pkg git https://github.com/you/pkg">
    <meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0; url=https://pkg.go.dev/example.com/pkg">
  </head>
  <body>
    Nothing to see here. Please <a href="https://pkg.go.dev/example.com/pkg">move along</a>.
  </body>
</html>

Host it on GitHub Pages or Netlify (both free with custom domains).

Option 2: Dynamic Server

Check the ?go-get=1 parameter:

func handler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if r.URL.Query().Get("go-get") == "1" {
        // Go tooling gets meta tags
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "text/html")
        fmt.Fprintf(w, `<meta name="go-import" content="example.com/pkg git https://github.com/you/pkg">`)
        return
    }
    // Humans get redirected
    http.Redirect(w, r, "https://pkg.go.dev/example.com/pkg", http.StatusFound)
}

This is what Google uses for google.golang.org/grpc.

Existing Tools:

  • vangen - Generate static HTML
  • sally - Uber’s production server

When It Makes Sense¶

After looking at who uses vanity import paths, the pattern is clear:

Use Case Makes Sense?
Large org with 10+ packages ✓
Might migrate from GitHub to GitLab ✓
Professional branding needed ✓
Small personal project (1-3 repos) ✗
Internal-only packages ✗
GitHub URL is already clean ✗

I’d say if you’re managing fewer than 5 packages and don’t plan to move VCS providers, stick with GitHub URLs. The overhead isn’t worth it.

But if you’re Uber with 50+ Go repos, having them all under go.uber.org/* makes a lot of sense.

The Elegance¶

Vanity import paths are beautifully simple: HTML meta tags + HTTP redirects. No complex infrastructure.

The clever bit? Same endpoint, different behavior:

  1. Go tooling (?go-get=1) → reads meta tags → clones from GitHub
  2. Humans (no parameter) → redirected to documentation

It’s optional for GitHub but available for custom domains. Only use it when you need it.

The real win: migrate from GitHub → GitLab → self-hosted without breaking downstream imports. Maximum flexibility, minimal code.

References¶

  • Remote import paths - Official spec
  • Module VCS Discovery - How Go discovers repositories
  • Vanity Import Paths in Go - Comprehensive guide
  • Go source: discovery.go, vcs.go

Appendix: The Caching Implementation¶

I mentioned Go caches the meta tag results. I was curious how that actually works, so I looked at the implementation in vcs.go:

// Global cache and mutex for thread-safe access
var (
    fetchCacheMu sync.Mutex
    fetchCache   = map[string]fetchResult{} // key is the import prefix
)

var fetchGroup singleflight.Group // Deduplicates concurrent requests

func metaImportsForPrefix(importPrefix string, ...) (*url.URL, []metaImport, error) {
    setCache := func(res fetchResult) (fetchResult, error) {
        fetchCacheMu.Lock()
        defer fetchCacheMu.Unlock()
        fetchCache[importPrefix] = res
        return res, nil
    }

    // Use singleflight to deduplicate concurrent requests
    resi, _, _ := fetchGroup.Do(importPrefix, func() (resi any, err error) {
        // Check cache first
        fetchCacheMu.Lock()
        if res, ok := fetchCache[importPrefix]; ok {
            fetchCacheMu.Unlock()
            return res, nil  // Cache hit!
        }
        fetchCacheMu.Unlock()

        // Cache miss - fetch from URL
        url, err := urlForImportPath(importPrefix)
        resp, err := web.Get(security, url)
        defer resp.Body.Close()

        imports, err := parseMetaGoImports(resp.Body, mod)
        return setCache(fetchResult{url: url, imports: imports, err: err})
    })
}

Two-level deduplication:

  1. Singleflight - If 10 goroutines request go.uber.org/zap simultaneously, only ONE HTTP request is made. Others wait for the result.
  2. Simple map cache - Once fetched, subsequent requests for go.uber.org/zap return cached results immediately (no HTTP call).

Example flow:

// First request: go.uber.org/zap
fetchCache = {} // empty
// → HTTP request to https://go.uber.org/zap?go-get=1
// → Store: {"go.uber.org/zap": {url, imports, err}}

// Second request: go.uber.org/zap
fetchCache = {"go.uber.org/zap": {...}}
// → Return cached result (no HTTP request)

// Concurrent requests:
// goroutine 1: requests go.uber.org/zap (makes HTTP call)
// goroutine 2: requests go.uber.org/zap (waits for goroutine 1)
// goroutine 3: requests go.uber.org/zap (waits for goroutine 1)
// → All three get the same result, only one HTTP request

The cache lives in memory for the duration of the go command execution. Not persisted to disk.

Simple but effective - prevents hammering vanity domains during dependency resolution.

entry.content:
Default Config Values are Actually Hidden Landmines¶

Published: Sunday, May 10, 2026 • 🏷️ golang • thoughts

The Setup¶

// config.go
func Load() Application {
    return Application{
        //...
        PrimaryAPI: PrimaryAPI{
            ApplicationID: EnvString("PRIMARY_API_APPLICATION_ID", "example-primary-api"),
            BaseURL:       EnvURL("PRIMARY_API_BASE_URL", "http://primary-service-test.mycomp.com"),
            TokenName:     EnvString("PRIMARY_API_TOKEN_NAME", "example-primary-api-write"),
        },
        SecondaryAPI: SecondaryAPI{
            ApplicationID: EnvString("SECONDARY_API_APPLICATION_ID", "example-secondary-api"),
            BaseURL:       EnvURL("SECONDARY_API_BASE_URL", "http://secondary-service-test.mycomp.com"),
            TokenName:     EnvString("SECONDARY_API_TOKEN_NAME", "example-secondary-api-write"),
        },
        // ...
    }
}

What Happened¶

A developer deployed a new service with several external API dependencies. The BaseURLs had default values pointing to TEST environment. Deployment succeeded, the service ran without errors, and everything looked fine.

Day later, we discovered data inconsistencies in PROD. The root cause: our service was silently calling TEST APIs from the PROD environment. TEST doesn’t have access to PROD services, but PROD can reach TEST (network asymmetry). So PROD was happily fetching stale test data instead of production data.

The deployment succeeded because the BaseURLs had defaults. No missing environment variables meant no startup failures. The configuration quietly fell back to TEST URLs.

The Fix¶

If a config value points to infrastructure (Database, API, Event Stream), it must be explicit - no defaults allowed. 

// config.go
func Load() Application {
    return Application{
        //...
        PrimaryAPI: PrimaryAPI{
            ApplicationID: EnvString("PRIMARY_API_APPLICATION_ID", "example-primary-api"),
            BaseURL:       MustEnvURL("PRIMARY_API_BASE_URL"),
            TokenName:     EnvString("PRIMARY_API_TOKEN_NAME", "example-primary-api-write"),
        },
        SecondaryAPI: SecondaryAPI{
            ApplicationID: EnvString("SECONDARY_API_APPLICATION_ID", "example-secondary-api"),
            BaseURL:       MustEnvURL("SECONDARY_API_BASE_URL"),
            TokenName:     EnvString("SECONDARY_API_TOKEN_NAME", "example-secondary-api-write"),
        },
        // ...
    }
}

// MustEnvURL returns URL from env var, panics if missing.
func MustEnvURL(key string) *url.URL {
    value := os.Getenv(key)
    if value == "" {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("missing required environment variable '%s'", key))
    }

    u, err := url.Parse(value)
    if err != nil {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("unable to convert %v to a url value", value))
    }

    return u
}

When Defaults Are Fine¶

Defaults work well for operational settings:

  • Application behavior: Log levels, timeouts, retry counts, page sizes
  • Development ergonomics: Debug flags, verbose mode, pretty-print
  • Feature flags: New features off by default
  • Non-critical integrations: Analytics, telemetry

These control how you communicate, not which system you target.

Type Example
✓ Safe RetryAttempts: EnvInt("RETRY_ATTEMPTS", 3)
✗ Dangerous BaseURL: EnvURL("API_BASE_URL", "https://api-test.company.com")

Rule: require config that determines infrastructure targets (fail-fast at startup) and allow defaults for operational behavior.

Building Resilient HTTP Clients in Go: A Middleware Journey¶

Published: Friday, May 08, 2026 • 🏷️ golang

Building reliable HTTP clients means handling failures gracefully. This post shows how a simple retry middleware evolved into a robust three-layer system: Cache, Retry, and RateLimitRetry.

The Starting Point: Basic Retry¶

Initially, we had just retry logic with exponential backoff:

func createHTTPClient(tracer trace.Tracer, timeout time.Duration) *http.Client {
    baseClient := &http.Client{Timeout: timeout}

    return middleware.WrapClient(baseClient,
        middleware.Retry(middleware.RetryConfig{
            MaxRetries: 3,
            Backoff: middleware.NewExponentialBackoff(
                500*time.Millisecond, // Initial interval
                5*time.Second,        // Max interval
                30*time.Second,       // Max elapsed time
            ),
            Tracer: tracer,
        }),
    )
}

This handles transient failures (5xx errors) but has limitations:

  • Every request hits the external API
  • Rate limits (429) get treated like any other retry
  • No awareness of Retry-After headers

The Evolution: Adding Cache + RateLimitRetry¶

The enhanced version adds two specialized middleware layers:

func createHTTPClient(tracer trace.Tracer, timeout time.Duration) *http.Client {
    baseClient := &http.Client{Timeout: timeout}

    return middleware.WrapClient(baseClient,
        middleware.Cache(middleware.CacheConfig{
            TTL:    10 * time.Second,
            Tracer: tracer,
        }),
        middleware.Retry(middleware.RetryConfig{
            MaxRetries: 3,
            Backoff: middleware.NewExponentialBackoff(
                500*time.Millisecond,
                5*time.Second,
                30*time.Second,
            ),
            Tracer: tracer,
        }),
        middleware.RateLimitRetry(middleware.RateLimitRetryConfig{
            MaxRetries:        2,
            MaxRetryAfterWait: 10 * time.Second,
            DefaultRetryAfter: 2 * time.Second,
            Tracer:            tracer,
        }),
    )
}

Middleware order matters: Cache → Retry → RateLimitRetry

Why This Design?¶

Cache first - When a response is cached, the request never reaches retry or rate limit layers. Cache hits return in ~1ms vs 100ms+ for API calls.

RateLimitRetry - HTTP 429 isn’t a failure, it’s intentional throttling. The Retry-After header tells you exactly when to retry - no guessing with exponential backoff. For 5xx errors, it passes through to the general Retry middleware.

Separation of concerns - Each middleware handles one failure type. OpenTelemetry tracing shows exactly which layer handled each request.

Scenarios: The Middleware in Action¶

All scenarios use the complete middleware chain shown above.

Scenario 0: Baseline¶

Happy path - request flows through all layers, succeeds.

Scenario 1: Cache Hit/Miss¶

First request (MISS): 150ms. Second request (HIT): instant.

Scenario 2: Retry with 5xx¶

Server returns 500 twice, then succeeds with exponential backoff.

Scenario 3: Rate Limit Handling¶

429 with Retry-After: 2 → waits 2s → retries → succeeds.

Scenario 4: Rate Limit Exhaustion¶

Persistent 429s exhaust retry limit, fails gracefully.

Scenario 5: 5xx Passes Through¶

RateLimitRetry passes 5xx to Retry (no RateLimitRetry spans). Success gets cached.

Scenario 6: Timeout¶

Client timeout exceeded - fails fast, no retry.

See It in Action¶

Want to see how these middleware patterns work in real code?
The complete implementation with a live demo is ready to run: demo-http-middleware-patterns

What You Get¶

  • Production-ready middleware - Cache, Retry, and RateLimitRetry using battle-tested libraries (jellydator/ttlcache, cenkalti/backoff)
  • Visual debugging - OpenTelemetry traces show exactly how requests flow through the middleware layers
  • 7 interactive scenarios - See cache hits, exponential backoff, rate limit handling, and edge cases in action

TL;DR¶

In my previous post I explained the need for common-make. Here I’m going to present main features which might motivate you to apply the similar approaches in your day-to-day work.

Main features:

  1. No manual work - after git clone, everything works out of the box
  2. Dependency auto-install - all related tools will be downloaded in background

After setup, developers get 20+ make targets (make help) including multi-arch builds, auto-linting, and code generation - all without configuration.

Typical workflow¶

Makefile setup¶

We assume each Go-service uses the following Makefile (see extended sample go-service-blueprint).

This file contains only the essentials:

# Capture built-in Make variables (required for 'make vars' to work)
VARS_OLD := $(.VARIABLES)

# ============================================
# Common Makefile Configuration
# ============================================
COMMON_MAKE_VERSION := v1.2.0
COMMON_MAKE_REPO := git@github.com:halyph/go-service-common-make.git

# Auto-download common-make if missing
.common-make/common.mk: .common-make/.version-$(COMMON_MAKE_VERSION)
    @echo "📦 Already downloaded"

.common-make/.version-$(COMMON_MAKE_VERSION):
    @echo "📦 Cloning common-make $(COMMON_MAKE_VERSION)..."
    @rm -rf .common-make
    @# Try quiet clone first (suppresses git warnings), fallback to verbose if it fails (for debugging)
    @git clone --depth=1 --branch $(COMMON_MAKE_VERSION) --single-branch --quiet $(COMMON_MAKE_REPO) .common-make 2>/dev/null || \
        git clone --depth=1 --branch $(COMMON_MAKE_VERSION) --single-branch $(COMMON_MAKE_REPO) .common-make || \
        (echo "❌ Failed to clone common-make repository" && exit 1)
    @rm -rf .common-make/.git
    @touch .common-make/.version-$(COMMON_MAKE_VERSION)
    @echo "✓ common-make $(COMMON_MAKE_VERSION) ready"

# ============================================
# Application Configuration
# ============================================
APPLICATION := go-service-blueprint

# ============================================
# Include Common Makefile
# ============================================
include .common-make/common.mk

Standardizing Go Build Systems Across 15 Microservices with Claude Code¶

Published: Thursday, Apr 23, 2026 • 🏷️ golang • claude code • make

TL;DR¶

I used Claude Code to standardize build systems across 15+ Go microservices, maintaining 100% test pass rates.

Key results:

  • 81% reduction in Makefile boilerplate (170 → 30 lines)
  • Developer onboarding: 1 hour → 15 minutes
  • Zero production incidents

The technique: Feed Claude Code reference repos using @../service-a/Makefile syntax - don’t ask it to invent, ask it to extract proven patterns.

The Problem: When Build Systems Diverge¶

Go lacks Maven, Gradle, or sbt equivalents. While Java has standardized build tools that enforce consistency, Go teams rely on:

  • Makefiles for build automation
  • External binaries like mockery (code generation) and golangci-lint (linting)
  • Tools installed either globally or project-local

This works fine for a single service. But when you have 10+ services, each 90% similar but 100% inconsistent, you end up with a maintenance nightmare.

The Developer Onboarding Problem¶

Here’s what a new developer experienced trying to run tests on their first day:

1. git clone <repo>
2. make test
   ❌ golangci-lint: command not found

3. brew install golangci-lint  # (installs wrong version)
4. make test
   ❌ Error: mockery: command not found

5. brew install mockery
6. make generate
   ❌ Mocks not found (expected in different folder)
7. make test
   ❌ Tests fail in CI (different tool versions)

8. 1 hour later: still not running

This happened to EVERY new team member.

The root causes:

  • Makefile duplication: ~170 lines per repo, 95% identical
  • Mock inconsistency: 50% of services didn’t commit mocks → CI randomly failed
  • Global tool dependencies: Version chaos across developer machines
  • Copy-paste errors: CI/CD configuration diverged over time

The Secret: Reference Repo Pattern¶

Don’t ask Claude Code to invent solutions - ask it to extract patterns from proven implementations.

Instead of:

“Claude, figure out how to build Go services”

We used:

“Claude, study these 3 working repos and extract common patterns”

@../service-a/Makefile
@../service-b/Makefile
@../service-c/Makefile

Why this works: Copies proven patterns, reduces hallucination risk, tests verify immediately.

The Journey: Two Phases¶

Phase 1: Standardize Individual Repos (8 repos)¶

The Approach:

  1. First migration: Manual + Claude Code on one service, document decisions in migration guide
  2. Parallel execution: Used tmux with 6-8 panes, each running one Claude Code session referencing @MIGRATION_GUIDE.md (30-45 minutes per service)

What got standardized:

  • Tools as code dependencies (see Manage Go CLI tools via Go modules and tools.go)
  • Mocks committed to repository (see Golang: Do you commit your generated mocks to repo?)
  • Multi-arch builds with single Dockerfile (amd64 + arm64)
  • Consistent Makefile structure

Phase 2: Extract Common Components (7 repos)¶

Claude Code analyzed 9 repositories and discovered Makefiles were 95% identical (~170 lines each): same build functions, Docker patterns, tools, and quality gates.

Result: Extracted to go-service-common-make

Architecture:

go-service-common-make/
├── common.mk              # Entry point
├── common.build.mk        # Multi-arch builds
├── common.docker.mk       # Docker buildx
├── common.tools.mk        # Tools installation
├── common.quality.mk      # Test, lint, generate
└── common.help.mk         # Help system

Per-repo Makefile:

COMMON_MAKE_VERSION := v1.0.0
COMMON_MAKE_REPO    := git@github.com:halyph/go-service-common-make.git

.common-make/common.mk: .common-make/.version-$(COMMON_MAKE_VERSION)
.common-make/.version-$(COMMON_MAKE_VERSION):
    @rm -rf .common-make
    @git clone --depth=1 --branch $(COMMON_MAKE_VERSION) \
               $(COMMON_MAKE_REPO) .common-make
    @rm -rf .common-make/.git
    @touch .common-make/.version-$(COMMON_MAKE_VERSION)

APPLICATION := my-service
include .common-make/common.mk

Phase 2 Results:

All services built successfully on first try. Nearly all tests passed—the one failure was pre-existing lint issue unrelated to migration.

Key Takeaways¶

What made this work:

  • Reference repos eliminate AI guesswork - Feed Claude proven implementations using @path/to/file syntax instead of asking it to invent solutions
  • Standardize first, extract later - Get individual repos working before creating shared components. This validates patterns before extracting them
  • Sub-agents for exploration - Used sub-agents when analyzing across 9+ repositories to avoid context limits in main session

entry.title: Automating Kubernetes ConfigMap Updates with Reloader
entry.content:
Automating Kubernetes ConfigMap Updates with Reloader¶

Published: Tuesday, Mar 31, 2026 • 🏷️ kubernetes

The Problem¶

Managing shared configuration across multiple Kubernetes services is error-prone:

  • Multiple PRs required to update each service
  • Easy to forget which services need updates
  • Separate CI/CD deployments for each service
  • High risk of inconsistency

Solution: Kubernetes ConfigMaps¶

Shared ConfigMaps are ideal, but by default ConfigMap updates don’t trigger pod restarts - pods keep running with stale values.

The solution: use a Kubernetes controller that automatically restarts pods when ConfigMaps change.

Reloader is a Kubernetes controller that automatically triggers rollouts when referenced ConfigMaps or Secrets are updated.

The updated process:

Impact:

  • Before: N pull requests, N deployments, N opportunities to forget
  • After: 1 pull request, 1 ConfigMap update, automatic rollout to all services

Implementation¶

Benefits:

  • Automatic service restarts when ConfigMaps change
  • Zero manual intervention
  • Battle-tested solution (9k+ GitHub stars)
  • Minimal changes to existing services

Future Enhancement: External Config Sync¶

For full automation, a ConfigSync operator could fetch configs from external APIs (e.g., GitHub raw URLs, REST API) and sync them to ConfigMaps. Combined with Reloader, this enables end-to-end automation:

External API → ConfigMap → Automatic Service Restart.

Sample¶

Note: The following YAML files use {{ VARIABLE }} placeholders for environment-specific values. Replace these with your actual values before deployment.

Reloader Deployment¶

# Reloader Complete Deployment - All-in-One
#
# What Reloader Monitors:
#   - ConfigMaps (enabled) - watches for changes and restarts workloads
#   - Secrets (disabled via --resources-to-ignore=secrets)
#
# Workload Types Configured:
#   - Deployments ✅ - standard stateless applications (THIS IS WHAT WE USE)
#   - StatefulSets ✅ - stateful applications with persistent storage
#   - DaemonSets ⚠️ - read-only (can monitor but won't restart them)
#   - CronJobs ❌ - ignored (see --ignored-workload-types flag)
#   - Jobs ❌ - ignored (see --ignored-workload-types flag)
#
# Note: DaemonSets have list/get permissions only (no update/patch)
# to avoid RBAC permission issues while keeping logs clean
#
# Expected Behavior:
#   ✅ Watches ConfigMaps in specified namespace (e.g. my-namespace)
#   ✅ Restarts Deployments/StatefulSets when their ConfigMaps change
#   ✅ Clean logs with no errors
#
# Deploy: kubectl apply -f reloader-complete.yaml
# Watch: kubectl logs -f deployment/reloader -n {{ NAMESPACE }}
# Verify: kubectl get pods -n {{ NAMESPACE }}
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ APPLICATION }}
  namespace: {{ NAMESPACE }}
  labels:
    application: {{ APPLICATION_ID }}
    component: controller
    team: {{ TEAM_ID }}
spec:
  replicas: {{ REPLICAS }}
  revisionHistoryLimit: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      application: {{ APPLICATION_ID }}
      component: controller
      team: {{ TEAM_ID }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        application: {{ APPLICATION_ID }}
        component: controller
        team: {{ TEAM_ID }}
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: reloader
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 65534
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      containers:
        - name: reloader
          image: "{{ DOCKER_REGISTRY }}/{{ IMAGE_PATH }}"
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          args:
            # Ignore secrets to avoid permission errors and only watch ConfigMaps
            - --resources-to-ignore=secrets
            - --log-format=json
            - --ignored-workload-types=jobs,cronjobs
            - --log-level={{ LOG_LEVEL }}

          # Namespace filtering - Choose ONE approach:
          #
          # Option 1: KUBERNETES_NAMESPACE env variable (recommended for explicit namespaces)
          #   - Use when: You know exact namespace names
          #   - Example: env var KUBERNETES_NAMESPACE="my-ns,another-ns"
          #   - Simpler, explicit list of namespaces
          #
          # Option 2: --namespace-selector flag (for dynamic label-based selection)
          #   - Use when: You want to select namespaces by labels
          #   - Example: --namespace-selector="env=production,team=myteam"
          #   - Automatically includes new namespaces matching labels
          #
          #   - --namespace-selector="kubernetes.io/metadata.name=myteam"                  # Comma separated namespace labels
          #   - --resource-label-selector="team=myteam,environment in (live,staging-main)" # Comma separated resource labels
          #   - --reload-on-create=true   # Add this line to enable reload on create
          #   - --reload-on-delete=true   # Add this line to enable reload on delete
          #   - --resources-to-ignore="secrets"
          env:
            - name: GOMAXPROCS
              valueFrom:
                resourceFieldRef:
                  resource: limits.cpu
                  divisor: '1'
            - name: GOMEMLIMIT
              valueFrom:
                resourceFieldRef:
                  resource: limits.memory
                  divisor: '1'
            - name: RELOADER_NAMESPACE
              valueFrom:
                fieldRef:
                  fieldPath: metadata.namespace
            - name: RELOADER_DEPLOYMENT_NAME
              value: {{ APPLICATION }}
            # Monitor specific namespace(s) - see comments above for --namespace-selector alternative
            - name: KUBERNETES_NAMESPACE
              value: "{{ WATCH_NAMESPACES }}" # Single namespace, or comma-separated: "ns1,ns2"
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 9090
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /live
              port: http
            timeoutSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
            successThreshold: 1
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /metrics
              port: http
            timeoutSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
            successThreshold: 1
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            capabilities:
              drop:
                - ALL
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          resources:
            limits:
              cpu: {{ CPU_LIMIT }}
              memory: {{ MEMORY_LIMIT }}
            requests:
              cpu: {{ CPU_REQUEST }}
              memory: {{ MEMORY_REQUEST }}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: {{ NAMESPACE }}

---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: reloader-role
rules:
  - apiGroups:
      - ""
    resources:
      - configmaps
    verbs:
      - list
      - get
      - watch
      - create
      - update
  - apiGroups:
      - "apps"
    resources:
      - deployments
      - statefulsets
    verbs:
      - list
      - get
      - update
      - patch
  - apiGroups:
      - "apps"
    resources:
      - daemonsets
    verbs:
      - list
      - get
  - apiGroups:
      - "extensions"
    resources:
      - deployments
    verbs:
      - list
      - get
      - update
      - patch
  - apiGroups:
      - "extensions"
    resources:
      - daemonsets
    verbs:
      - list
      - get
  - apiGroups:
      - "batch"
    resources:
      - cronjobs
    verbs:
      - list
      - get
  - apiGroups:
      - "batch"
    resources:
      - jobs
    verbs:
      - create
      - delete
      - list
      - get
  - apiGroups:
      - ""
    resources:
      - events
    verbs:
      - create
      - patch

---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: reloader-role-binding
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: reloader-role
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: reloader
    namespace: {{ NAMESPACE }}
---
# ServiceAccount for Reloader
#
# Why this is required:
#   - Provides identity for Reloader pod to authenticate with Kubernetes API
#   - Connected to ClusterRole via ClusterRoleBinding for RBAC permissions
#   - Grants permissions to watch ConfigMaps and update/patch Deployments
#   - Without this, pod runs with default ServiceAccount (no permissions)
#
# Used in deployment.yaml: spec.serviceAccountName: reloader
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: reloader
  namespace: {{ NAMESPACE }}

Simple App with Reloader Auto-Reload¶

# This demonstrates how Reloader automatically restarts pods on ConfigMap changes
#
# Prerequisites: Deploy reloader-complete.yaml first
#
# Deploy: kubectl apply -f example-auto-reload.yaml
# Watch: kubectl logs -f deployment/app-auto-reload -n my-namespace
# Update: kubectl patch configmap app-config-auto -n my-namespace --type merge -p '{"data":{"APP_VERSION":"2.0.0"}}'
# Observe: Reloader will trigger a rolling restart automatically!

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: my-namespace

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config-auto
  namespace: my-namespace
data:
  APP_NAME: "MyApp"
  APP_VERSION: "1.0.0"
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  FEATURE_FLAG_X: "false"

---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app-auto-reload
  namespace: my-namespace
  labels:
    app: app-auto-reload
  annotations:
    # Reloader will watch ALL ConfigMaps/Secrets used by this deployment
    reloader.stakater.com/auto: "true"

    # Alternative 1: Watch specific ConfigMaps only
    # configmap.reloader.stakater.com/reload: "app-config-auto"
    #
    # Alternative 2: Watch all ConfigMaps
    # configmap.reloader.stakater.com/auto: "true"
    #
    # IgnoreResourceAnnotation is an annotation to ignore changes in secrets/configmaps
    # reloader.stakater.com/ignore: "true"
    #
    # Comma separated list of configmaps that excludes detecting changes
    # configmaps.exclude.reloader.stakater.com/reload: "app-config-auto"

    # Allows to specify exactly which ConfigMaps should trigger a reload
    # configmap.reloader.stakater.com/reload: "my-config,shared-config"  

spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: app-auto-reload
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: app-auto-reload
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: ubuntu:24.04
          command:
            - /bin/sh
            - -c
            - |
              echo "================================================"
              echo "  Application Started"
              echo "  Pod: $HOSTNAME"
              echo "  Start Time: $(date)"
              echo "================================================"
              echo ""

              # Print initial ConfigMap values
              echo "=== Initial Configuration ==="
              for file in /config/*; do
                if [ -f "$file" ]; then
                  printf "  %-20s : %s\n" "$(basename "$file")" "$(cat "$file")"
                fi
              done
              echo "============================="
              echo ""

              echo "App is running..."
              echo "When ConfigMap changes, Reloader will restart this pod."
              echo ""

              # Keep running and show uptime periodically
              while true; do
                uptime_sec=$(awk '{print int($1)}' /proc/uptime)
                echo "[$(date '+%H:%M:%S')] App is healthy (uptime: ${uptime_sec}s)"
                sleep 30
              done
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config-volume
              mountPath: /config
              readOnly: true
          resources:
            limits:
              cpu: "100m"
              memory: "64Mi"
            requests:
              cpu: "10m"
              memory: "64Mi"
      volumes:
        - name: config-volume
          configMap:
            name: app-config-auto
